lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you met the three powers of government. Which one makes the laws? (Parliament.) Today: how an idea becomes a law, step by step, and why debate matters.

Ideas for new laws come from many places: the government's plans, members of parliament, campaigns and petitions, problems in the news, or court cases that show a law is unclear. A plan for a new law is called a bill.

In the UK Parliament a bill goes through stages in the House of Commons. First reading: its title is read out. Second reading: the main debate. Committee stage: it is checked line by line. Then come a report stage and a third reading.

picture.title: A bill in the UK Parliament

lesson.text: Then the other House, the House of Lords, goes through the same stages. It can suggest changes, and the bill may pass back and forth until both Houses agree. Finally the monarch signs it, royal assent, and it becomes an Act: a law.

Royal assent is now a formality: a monarch last refused it in 1708, under Queen Anne. In the USA, a bill passes both houses of Congress. Then the president signs it or vetoes it. Congress can overturn a veto with two-thirds of each house.

Why so many stages? Debate tests a law before it affects millions of people. Members point out problems, speak for the people they represent and propose amendments (changes), and committees ask experts. A rushed law can be a bad law.

Most decisions are made by majority votes: more than half. In the House of Commons, with 650 members, a group needs 326 seats for a majority. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland also have their own parliament or assembly for some laws.

Try it in the world: turn a server rule into a law. Write it as a bill, read it out and debate it with friends. Amend it if needed, vote, and put the final Act on a sign. Next: constitutions and rights.

exercises.hint: It is what a law is called before it passes.
choices: a plan for a new law
exercises.explain: A plan for a new law, debated and voted on in Parliament.

exercises.prompt: Which stage is the main debate in the House of Commons?
exercises.hint: At the first reading only the title is read.
exercises.explain: The second reading: the main debate on the bill's ideas, after the first reading of its title.

exercises.prompt: In the UK, a bill must pass both Houses of Parliament.
exercises.hint: Think of the Commons and the Lords.
exercises.explain: True: both the Commons and the Lords, then royal assent.

exercises.hint: It is the very last step.
choices: the monarch's agreement that makes it law
exercises.explain: The monarch's formal agreement: the bill becomes an Act.

exercises.prompt: Where can ideas for new laws come from?
exercises.hint: Think of all the people who can raise a problem.
exercises.explain: From the government, members, campaigns, petitions, the news and court cases.

exercises.prompt: Put these stages in the House of Commons in order.
exercises.hint: The title is read first, then the main debate, then the close check.
exercises.explain: First reading, second reading, committee, report, third reading.

exercises.prompt: The House of Commons has 650 members. How many seats make a majority, more than half?
exercises.explain: Half of 650 is 325; one more is 326.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
matches: checks a bill line by line
exercises.hint: One changes, one refuses, one is the result, one checks.
exercises.explain: Amendment: a change. Veto: a refusal. Act: a law. Committee: checks line by line.

exercises.hint: It comes after the main debate.
exercises.explain: The committee stage, where the bill is checked line by line.

exercises.prompt: The last time a monarch refused royal assent was in 1708.
exercises.explain: True: Queen Anne, 1708; since then it has always been given.

exercises.prompt: The US Senate has 100 members. To overturn a veto, at least two-thirds must agree. If all vote, what is the fewest votes that is enough?
exercises.hint: Find two-thirds, then go up to the next whole vote.
exercises.explain: Two-thirds of 100 is 66.67; the next whole vote is 67.

exercises.prompt: Why do bills go through so many stages?
exercises.hint: What could go wrong with a rushed law?
choices: so problems are found before it becomes law
to make laws slow for no reason
exercises.explain: Each stage is a chance to find problems and improve the bill before it affects everyone.

exercises.prompt: Once a law is made, it can never be changed.
exercises.hint: Can Parliament pass a new law about an old one?
exercises.explain: False: Parliament can change or cancel a law with a new Act.

choices: to improve a bill or fix a problem
exercises.explain: To improve a bill, fix problems in it, or speak for the people they represent.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: in the House of Commons, or after it?
exercises.hint: A bill passes the Commons, then goes to the Lords, then to the monarch.
exercises.explain: In the Commons: first reading, second reading, committee. After: the Lords' debate and amendments, then royal assent.
